rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.4 and 3.1 - the authors build a GMS/MODFLOW groundwater model of Qalyubia Governorate, calibrate it in steady state against 11 observation wells (2014 RIGW heads, Fig. 7) and verify against 5 further points (Fig. 8), then run flood-irrigation base and 'modern irrigation' district scenarios (Table 3, Fig. 10).
rows.notes: The study does not generate its own evidence that drip (or modern) irrigation produces lower recharge than flood irrigation; the lower recharge is an input assumption. Section 3.2 states that because of the high water efficiency of modern irrigation the recharge in a district switched to modern irrigation is set to zero, and pumping is cut by 40% based on a cited water-saving range [16]. The reported result (water table lowered by 10-50 cm, most in Tokh with a shallow clay cap) is the model's response to that assumed zero recharge, and the modern-irrigation scenario is not compared with any observations (only the flood-irrigation base case is calibrated/verified). The technology is generic 'modern/water-saving irrigation' rather than drip specifically, although drip is named as one of the modern methods. The authors do state a mechanism (clay-cap depth governs the magnitude of the decline) and a limitation (future domestic/industrial demand not considered), but since Q2 is 'no' these are not credited. No dispersion measures; only ranges of head decline across districts.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references and author biographies). Study is a regional MODFLOW scenario analysis; the key recharge difference between flood and modern irrigation is assumed (zero recharge under modern irrigation) rather than measured or derived.
